utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting for quite a long time in The Hague. Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Krsnik. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you. Thank you for everything. And I will now continue with my examination. Before commencing, I would ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to inform the witness of a decision and perhaps it would be best to go into private session, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krsnik: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness we spoke about the negotiations in Jablanica at the last hearing and we spoke about Sovici. I would like to finish with this today and I would like to show you a cassette and just show you two photographs, so that you can become familiar with them and then we can move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, there is just one sentence I would like to say. First of all I need to provide the Judge with some information. In the documents that I had and the reports that I had which were all muddled up, I said that that meeting was held on the 5th of May, which is not correct because the report was written on that date, on the 5th of May, but the meeting took place one day earlier, that is to say on the 4rth of May. This is just for the sake of precision. That's one thing. And the second matter is that I am a little -- I regret that the Judge said that the two reports were more important than my testimony. That's what I understood. In the following two or five minutes, or in that case, I misunderstood something but if necessary, I will write -- I'm quite capable of writing a report here for about two minutes which relates to this part which I gave testimony about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If I may, Dr. Bagaric, what I said on Tuesday, I believe, was that it was a pity that the two reports which we had referred to the other two villages because the village you visited is the subject matter of the indictment. That's what I said. I didn't say that the reports were more important. I said it was a great pity that you hadn't actually written the report which we had, but as you said, we have you here to give your testimony. It's just it might have refreshed your memory to see a contemporaneous report but that's the only comment I was making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And if I may add, that we believe that the live testimony in this Tribunal is more important than any report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much, and I would like to apologise to Judge Clark. Obviously, I misunderstood her. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could the technicians please show the video which we prepared? It's Exhibit -- it's video clip number 5 from the Prosecution. The OTP. And I will then say-- because we've already seen, we've already viewed this video it might not be necessary to show the entire video but just part of it and then we will ask certain questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this video clip unfortunately has no sound, has no text, although you can see the people are speaking in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here. We can pause here. We won't need it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, can you remember anything with regard to this cassette? Is that the meeting, that event, the visit to the school in Sovici that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to follow this carefully, this cassette, and to recognise myself. I think I have the impression that I am -- that I recognise myself in that group. However, at the moment, I can't categorically state that that was me but I think that one person in the uniform, I think that was myself. But I think it is more important or rather equally important I think the fact that we visited that area is equally important and that we visited it together with UN representatives and with BH Army representatives, and that the representatives of the army, after that visit, they were very, very content. They didn't find any of the elements that the HVO had been accused of, that the HVO had been accused of having committed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Bagaric, I apologise, Dr. Bagaric, could you remember whether it was on that day, what you saw on the cassette, was that the visit? Did you recognise anyone else on the video? If not I can show it once more because I recognised you. Did you recognise anyone else out of the HVO -- among the HVO delegation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so but I don't think it would be bad to show the video again, if there is more to be seen and then I might be able to give a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. definite answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the technicians to start again from the beginning and if the lights could perhaps be adjusted, if the intensity of the lights could be reduced a bit so that we may see this video more easily?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you say whom you can recognise in the video, if you do recognise someone? And also whether that was -- that took place on the day concerned, the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm in the tape. I've got a Red Cross mark on my left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pause and rewind a bit? And would the technician be so kind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's no issue whether he was at this particular meeting. It's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But we would like to see it any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's fine, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you rewind a bit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could comment perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well the person facing us on his left shoulder, he has a sign of the medical headquarters or rather of the International Red Cross. If you show the cassette, the video, then you will see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first man on the stairs, the first man whose face you can see? Well, we can show it, we can carry on showing it and then please say whom else that you recognise. And that was on the 4th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 4th of May, yes. After the meeting in Jablanica, in UNPROFOR's headquarters, UNPROFOR's base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please continue showing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, now the sign -- the insignia can be seen.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see Petkovic there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person writing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be so kind and rewind it a bit? Because yesterday, you weren't sure either. Could the technicians please rewind it a bit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that's Rasim Delic but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this gentleman who is facing us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I couldn't say who he is at this moment. I can't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Perhaps we don't need the video any more. The important thing was that you recognised yourself and that that was the event in question. I have also prepared two photographs but I don't think it's necessary to show them any more. Perhaps one, just one photograph. That's Exhibit 8.3. So would the usher be so kind as to show you the photograph and could you tell us whether you know what the photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, last time I clearly said, and I would like to repeat that now, I want to be absolutely clear and honest when giving testimony here, and I won't make any assumptions of any kind. We passed through Doljani and through Sovici. I think that this is Sovici but I can't state so for certain. I think that it's Sovici but it's really not a problem to establish whether this is Sovici or not. I was travelling in an armoured personnel carrier and I didn't have such a panorama in front of me. We are talking about events that took place over ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you go from Jablanica towards Sovici, which is the first place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that first of all you come to Doljani and then Sovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all, as far as this subject is concerned. Thank you, usher. I'd like to move on to another subject. Could you tell this Trial Chamber what the relation with the Muslims was, with the Muslims in Mostar, with regard to help, cooperation in hospitals, aid? Did you have any contact with Arif Pasalic and with the eastern part of Mostar? And perhaps we could prepare the documents for this immediately. I'm going to ask the Registrar if she would be so kind as to prepare the documents D1/352, 351, 356, 380, 353, 378, and 355. I'm going to ask you to look at these documents and whenever you talk about a certain document, please mention its number first. You will find it in the bottom right side of the page and then you give us the comment, the document need not be read because it speaks for itself but can you please briefly comment on any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please start immediately after this meeting, i.e., after the return from Konjic and Jablanica, so that was a few days later, or maybe even on the following day or two days later. We doctors were very displeased and very dissatisfied with the Bosniak side, Muslim side, which did not allow us to go to these villages where we knew were -- there were many injured and killed people. So we expressed that dissatisfaction in the form of a protest. I did not know what to do so we wrote to international organisations. We appealed for assistance. We organised a press conference, to which we invited the eastern side and we appealed to their cooperation because we had a foreboding that the situation would go from bad to worse. So this position was dictated by us from the HVO who were doctors, and I thought that we had the right to claim certain things, as doctors, and in order for us to confirm our position as doctors, and to confirm that we were doing what we were supposed to do, that we were treating everybody. I launched several initiatives for establishing ties among the medical personnel on both sides of Mostar, which already at the time was divided because the army had already been formed, their doctors already were on the strength of their units, and in a certain way, I wanted to establish ties. I thought that I could prevent a conflict or maybe if not prevent, then its consequences could be mitigated if the doctors teamed up together and if they held a front, and I said that openly and this was aired on all the media, on both the western side and the eastern side, and I got a reply by Mr. Arif Pasalic, who I can't give you precisely what he said before I see the document. But in any case, Mr. Pasalic said, "Okay, you are offering us cooperation. Give us this and that. Give us medicines, give us equipment, give us personnel," and so on and so forth. I'll try -- and if these are -- the documents that I have I in front of you, I will try to comment on these documents and I'll try to clarify each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I believe you are talking about document D1/352 and D1/351.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I apologise. I don't know before I actually see the documents, I don't have -- still have them in front of me. In front of me, I have several documents which unfortunately are not complete. Some of these documents, for example, document 351, in which Mr. Arif Pasalic wrote on the 5th of June, 1993, and we are talking about the period after the events that I previously described, excuse me, I have to put these papers in a time order. Here I can see a document dating back to the 3rd of June, in which I say with reference to information on the lack of medicaments and medical supplies in the eastern part of the town controlled by you, we are ready to provide you immediately and unconditionally. So I'm talking about document D1/352 but there was another document which at this moment, I don't have, and it is relevant to the request by Mr. Pasalic to give him medicines. On the 3rd of June, I wrote back with reference to information on the lack of medicaments and medical supplies in the eastern part of the town, we are ready to provide you immediately and unconditionally with the indispensable medicines. And then on the 5th of 6, I received a document from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., from Arif Pasalic, he sent it to me, i.e., to us, in which he states exactly what they needed. That was on the 5th of June. There is also an order dating backs to the 7th of June, 1993, this is D1/356, in which we issued an order to give medicines to -- medications to the BH Army according to specification. And this document shows just one example of such a specification of medicaments which were issued. These are D1/380 and there is another document D1/355, in which is actually a reply, our reply to one of the requests and according to our reply, we were ready, we had prepared medicaments, we had given them to UNPROFOR for transport and we also explained why we could not send a team of doctors to the other side. And the reason was the following: Since the hospital in the western part of Mostar was much better equipped than the one in the eastern part of Mostar, we had a huge lack of personnel, a lot of doctors had left the hospital. That is why it says in this document, "With regard to the teams of documents, we would like to inform you that we do not have any volunteers, neither among the Muslim nor Croat personnel." And we also say that our capacities are not high and so on and so forth. And I also explain that what -- that the conditions for caring for the wounded population were much better here than there and that is why we propose you for the Nth time to send all your wounded to HVO war hospitals where they shall be given the same treatment as given to it our combatants in accordance with the Hippocratic oath and medical ethics. The identical treatment is guaranteed to you by the HVO, supreme medical headquarters, and myself personally and this was signed by Colonel Tugomir Gveric and myself. So this is a set of documents which are clear proof on cooperation with the eastern side, i.e., our attempt to extend our hand to them, to calm the situation, and our attempt to establish ties irrespective of the conflict, because doctors always thought, me personally including, that this conflict between Muslims and Croats is unnecessary and that it will result in nothing but victims, and that later on proved to be correct. There is another document in this set, I think it was on my table here last time before we broke the session, and it was our offer to the eastern side to offer the services of our hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be interrupting you. This is a document that I wanted to show you later on. And can I please ask our Madam Registrar to give the witness D1/362, to the witness. I.e., 1/371 and 1/373. I believe that one of these documents is the one that you were referring to. I don't know it off my head. That's all I propose, three documents, and you'll be able to see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were numerous attempts primarily for the doctors to do their job and to help each other, to treat everybody equally across the board. That's one thing. Another thing, we thought that it would be mutually beneficial, that it would be a great service to the eastern part of Mostar, where the situation was even worse, and we also thought that such a move could contribute to the situation in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina being -- becoming calmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the same time, we Croats were in an equally bad situation in central Bosnia. That's why. We thought that this example of cooperation in Mostar could have spread and could have extended to Travnik, Bugojno, Zepce, Zenica, and everywhere else. In front of me, I finally have, Your Honours, this request number D1/362. I believe that this request and if this is not too pretentious to say, I believe that this is a historical document. During the worst conflicts which were under way after a number of attempts on the part of doctors to establish ties in order to mitigate suffering, we come to the date 16 September, 1993, and unfortunately, a long time had lapsed before our initial request and this request but we did not know when the war would stop, whether it would stop at all. In this request, I am writing not to Pasalic but to UNPROFOR, to the Spanish Battalion, and in this request I tell them, we ask to you mediate in the offer to the Muslim side for admission and treatment of civilians, particularly women and children, to the regional war hospital in Mostar, as well as other HVO hospitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, kindly, if you could slow down. Please understand that this is all translated into two languages, and it is very important that your testimony be conveyed as well -- as good as possible. It is very difficult if you don't speak slowly. Please slow down. Whatever you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say is translated into two languages.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, it says that Muslims are guaranteed the same treatment as our civilians and injured. We proposed that our work is controlled by the International Red Cross, EC monitors and UNPROFOR. We are doing this for one and only one reason, and that is the humanitarian reason. So my concept was that we could, contrary to every logic of the war and contrary to the rules of the war, because this hospital was in the middle of the city, I thought that we could put our hospital under the UN control. This would have been done by UN guaranteeing for the security and safety of the hospital, that nobody could enter the hospital without their approval. The UN had enough strength in Mostar to implement that. They had enough armoured carriers to encircle the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, Dr. Bagaric, once again. Dr. Bagaric, once again, I apologise, I had to warn you. I understand you absolutely well, all of us who understand Croatian can follow you but we have noticed, and I have experienced that if our translators, interpreters, who are trying to follow you and convey the message, sometimes your message will be lost in translation and the transcript will convey a completely different message. Please bear that in it mind when you give your testimony. The Honourable Court cannot follow you for various reasons because they are not familiar with the area as well as we are, and please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I have the impression that I have already -- that you have already lost patience with me because this testimony has taken a long time, and that is maybe the explanation why I am speeding up. I shall repeat just briefly and I will -- and on that note, we thought that the consequences of the war could be mitigated, that we could contribute towards the end of the war between the two sides of -- both of which were nothing but the victims of the conflict in the area of the former Yugoslavia. Here I mean the Muslims and the Croats. Unfortunately, everybody was the victim of that war. We thought that we could offer our hospital as a symbol and as a reality, that we -- that UN -- UNPROFOR forces could protect this institution from all those who found our offer unacceptable. We also thought that it would have been good for the International Red Cross to enter the hospital and to control its work. And we thought that this would gain us the trust of the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I have to interrupt you. We do not have much more time. I believe that we only have about half an hour and there are two or three other things that I would like to ask you. I just want to ask you, we heard testimony here that you and the medical headquarters, that you offered the services of your hospital but it was in the front line and it was very hypocritical of you to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not a comment it is a question? We heard the testimony in this courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to make a similar objection that I made the other day. It is not necessary or in our respectful submission appropriate for counsel to make characterisations of prior testimony. He can simply put questions to the witness. I also believe it's not a proper characterisation of prior evidence to use the word hypocritical. I don't recall any witness using that terminology. And again I object to the argumentative nature of the questions put, neutral questions, factual questions can very simply be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, just ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I have the right, as counsel, to contradict -- I have the right to contradiction. These are the institutes which have existed since Roman law and all the legal systems have adopted it, both the Anglo-Saxon as well as the continental law. This witness is here to refute some allegations, whether he's going to refute them or not, we will hear from him. We will hear it in his testimony but we were all here, we were present to hear the testimony, according to which the hospital was offered but the Muslims did not want to expect that because it was hypocritical. Maybe it was not the word that was used but they knew exactly that that hospital could not be used because it was on the very front line in the city of Mostar. I believe that this is what was said, we also remember who said it, and I would like to ask Dr. Bagaric whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you ever the full right to contradict any testimony by the Prosecution's witness, but if there is an objection from the other side, I believe that you better ask simple questions. Eventually the result is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your instructions. I'm sure to follow them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you please reply to the answer whether this hospital indeed was not in service and whether it indeed was on the very front line?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said during my testimony that the hospital was on the front line. It was on the very line of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Honourable Court how many hospitals were there in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do not interrupt me. So the hospital was on the line. However, that hospital that we referred to as the war hospital, because it worked under the war circumstances, treated all patients, civilians and soldiers, and it was located, I believe, in five different places, some of which were less safe and the others were more safe. When we offered the services of the hospital, we did not choose and we did not make a distinction. We did not say we are going to give this part to you and we are going to keep this part to ourselves. We offered the services of the same hospital where we treated ours, so to say, and who is the one to say who is ours, who is anybody else's. So our wounded, we offered the services of that same hospital to everybody else, to bear the same risks and to benefit from the same results of treatment. Therefore, the allegation that it was hypocritical to offer those services can only be answered by a question. Is it not hypocritical when somebody asks for medical supplies, not to give them to him? Is it also hypocritical that if somebody needs a hospital, not to offer it to him? And you are in a position to do so. At the end of the day, is it not hypocritical that after this war, that we went through in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are again wars being waged all over the world, and again people get killed in the same way, have the same needs for medical treatment and our experience with that, and our messages in connection with that, are not being taken on board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, can you please answer me this? Have you ever received any answer, either via UNPROFOR or through any other mediator about that cooperation? Was that cooperation ever implemented? What happened?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received a reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. So that hospital which was on the front line, is it -- its name the old surgical centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, its name is the old surgical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it in service all the time or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used all the time, throughout the entire war, that surgical department was where people were operated upon, where they were treated, and then the injured -- the injured people would be referred to the hospital on the hill, which was much safer at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether you did anything else, whether you undertook anything else with international organisations in order to establish cooperation? I would like to ask Madam Registrar to prepare 350, 358 and 377.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war in Mostar, there were a number of attempts on our part in order to implement and do good with the help of international organisations, in order to help people whoever came to us doctors in the HVO or me personally during the war in Mostar, and whoever had a proposal for us as to what should be done, what could be done, in order to reduce the suffering and the pain, would have received our cooperation. We would participate in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please comment on these documents, everybody in the courtroom has these documents and they can read them for themselves.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, document D1/350 and document D1/358, are very important documents which testify to our attempts, even before the conflict with the Muslim side started, so these documents go back to the end of 1992. Mostar was visited by Mr. Robert Simon. He was President of the International American, I believe, organisation, IMC which stands for the International Medical Corps. He had a proposal for us. He told us we should express our willingness and interest to establish cooperation between us doctors, Croats and Muslims alike, that is the Croatian Defence Council and the BH Army. I took the opportunity, because I was a member of the parliament at the time, and I addressed Mr. Mile Akmadzic, who was at the time the Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I asked him, in document D1/358, to mediate and to offer to the chief of the BH Army, the chief of the medical personnel of that army, cooperation on our behalf, and that is the Exhibit D1/350, in which I requested -- I asked my colleague to write a document which would show our common wish for cooperation, and I told him I would co-sign that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to Mr. Simon? Did you inform him of the course that that operation was taking, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, Dr. Simon made certain efforts to help both the Croats and the Muslims. However, he didn't obtain that document signed by the two of us, because once again, I didn't have an answer. I didn't have a reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Simon make such a request? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he went to the Croatian embassy in America, I don't know how, through what line. He asked for contact with some of the doctors, some of the Croatian doctors in Bosnia. The reasons he gave were that he had had experience -- that he had had experience as a doctor in many international conflicts, and he said that after visiting Bosnia, he would probably give testimony before the American congress with regard to the situation in Bosnia. He thought that if we reached such an agreement, we would be unable to prevent any possible conflict, and that he would give testimony before the congress and we would get international help for our cooperation. Even if this only consisted of verbal support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you ever anything else to say? Because I would like to move on to another subject. The break is approaching.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm under a lot of pressure because time is short. There is also a story, one of many stories, about Mostar, and which relates to cooperation with individuals. For example, there is a well known story about Sally Baker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you about that, but if we have finished with this subject, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned Sally Baker, could the Registrar please prepare documents D1/349 and document D1/383? And then could you inform the Trial Chamber of Sally Baker, tell them who Sally Baker is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sally Baker is one of -- one of the many persons who went to that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. war area and tried to help and to reduce the suffering, et cetera. Among other things, she asked for authorisation, or rather for help, to go to the eastern side of Mostar and to assist, provide with aid, or rather withdraw and treat in hospitals several children who were ill on the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Could we also show document D1/388 and put it on the ELMO? Those are photographs from that book. D1/388. That's not the document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first of all like to comment on this document, D1/349.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's part of a series of documents that I had to issue in order to provide some kind of aid, to provide each other with some kind of aid. Sally Baker didn't have a vehicle. She asked us for a vehicle. I explained that we had about 80 vehicles that had been destroyed in the course of the conflict in Mostar and that we had no vehicles. But she said, "In that case, I can't go to the other side." I had no choice. I thought that the mission was an important one and that it was my duty to help her. So I ordered that she be given a vehicle. That happened on about 3 occasions I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the photographs on your right-hand side and could you say -- could you tell us what they depict? And here you've been called "Baby brigadier." Could you comment on that? Did you have the rank of brigadier and why "Baby brigadier"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think baby, well that's something she wrote in the book because at the time I was ten years younger, and in her opinion, she thought I was some kind of a child who was in the war, who was helping, who was treating patients, et cetera. The second photograph is a photograph taken just before she left for the eastern side, before she went to the eastern side. What is most interesting here is perhaps the fact that she succeeded in taking -- in bringing in about six children in one ambulance, and their mothers too. And it's very important to say that when she brought them over to our side, she wanted to deliver them to UNPROFOR and have UNPROFOR take them somewhere, where they could be treated. But UNPROFOR refused to do so. So once again, she contacted me, and asked me for help. I suggested the hospital in Mostar, but the relatives or rather the children's mothers wanted to leave Mostar and go to Split. At that point, I asked the chief nurse of the Split hospital, a good guardian angel of all those from Bosnia-Herzegovina, her name was Marija Zupanovic, who took in those children and their mothers, and they continued to be provided with treatment in the hospital in Split. And some of them went abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another subject, if we can deal with it before the break. And I would like to ask Your Honours to allow me to continue for about ten or 15 minutes and I think that I will then be able to conclude the matter. Should I have a break now or should I continue? Very well. Let's turn to the 9th of May, 1993, in Mostar. 9th of May, 1993. What are you aware of? Where were you? It would be best for you to talk about it, if we finished with the subject of Sally Baker. If there is anything else you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the moment because I think it would be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mention the 9th of May, are you referring to the date when the conflict in Mostar began?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I don't know the dates any more.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right? Well, one day earlier, a few days prior to that date, I noticed, and the doctors who were born in Mostar, who were born down there, told me of this, they told me that the situation in the town was such that there was a possibility of a conflict between the army and the HVO. They said that this was possible. I didn't want to believe this. But I think it was on the 9th of August, a day earlier [As translated], I went to the Main Staff of the HVO, and I asked them whether they had any information about the possibility of a conflict, because I thought that we had to be prepared, I thought that we doctors had to be present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to interrupt you, because in the transcript it didn't say that -- it doesn't say that you were there a day earlier on the 8th. I can't follow. And it says August, not May. So you can see what sort of problems we have on a daily basis. This is why I'm asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the interpreters very well and those who are typing this. I think it is most difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are quite right. Please repeat that briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 8th, I was in the staff, the 8th of May, 1993. We doctors, we are always ready, but I asked them whether it was possible that we might have to be engaged in a more -- at a more intense level. They told me, "Doctor, sleep peacefully. There will be no conflict." They weren't expecting a conflict. I can claim this categorically. I went to a hotel in Citluk and together with several other doctors, after a certain period of time, after a certain time, I went to sleep, naturally. And early in the morning, I was called and they asked me where I was, given that there was a war going on in Mostar. I was really very surprised. Several of us entered Mostar. We went towards the hospital on the hill where, let's say, my headquarters was located, and the shooting in Mostar, or rather the noise of weapons, I don't know what kind of weapons, I'm not in a position -- I'm not capable of identifying them, the noise was incredible, and I think that on that day, there were about 100 seriously wounded people, and then the days followed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many people died and what sort of weapons caused these deaths mostly, that you are aware of personally?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally take care of people and I didn't personally operate on them, but at the time, the greatest number of those who died or were seriously wounded were people who had been hit directly in the head. I remembered afterwards, after that, I suggested that -- or I advised officers to order their soldiers to wear helmets. I wore a helmet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember the number of people who were hit in the head, if you know this? I won't insist on it, if you can't say so. More or less were these civilians or soldiers? If you know, naturally.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, I don't know the number but it's not a problem by going through the hospital protocol, it's not a problem to establish this, to check this information, but I think that there were about 100 people who died or who were seriously, very seriously wounded, and this concerned direct hits to the head or to the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think this will be a leading question and there won't be any objections from my colleague. So can we conclude that these people were wounded by snipers can we conclude -- come to this conclusion on the basis of that information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what sort of wounds were in question, how these people had been wounded so I think it's not necessary to comment further on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bagaric. It is now time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I assume this is the right time for a break. I would like to ask you for another 15 minutes after the break and I have about another two subjects and after that, I will have concluded with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go to private session just for one moment so I don't inadvertently disclose something that shouldn't be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now put a question to you, later I shall hand you over to the Prosecutor. Have you heard about some detention centre or prison which was called the Heliodrom? What do you know about this place? And did you take any action with regard to this place, your doctors, et cetera? Mr. Bagaric put your headphones on your head like I have so that they don't fall off all the time. You see, you can press them here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the question is whether I've heard about the Heliodrom? Of course, unfortunately I have. It would be far better if no one had heard about a single detention centre. However, since we are talking about the Heliodrom detention centre, yes, I was there on one occasion. I went there personally. What can I say about that place? What I think is important to this Tribunal is that at the beginning of the conflict between the BH Army and the Croats, there was a lack of confidence, a terrible lack of confidence between the population, among the population, in Mostar. And certainly, in the units of the HVO, which had a mixed composition, so the lack of trust in those units was intense. So when members of the BH Army, for this or for that reason, left the HVO or rather in many cases unfortunately they agreed to do so in the course of the evening, and they turned their weapons against their colleagues, against people who had been their colleagues before, and then there turned into a lack of trust towards the Muslims in general in the town, and vice versa. So there was mistrust of the Muslims, with regard to the Croats. And I think that the reason for this is that, well, people were gathered, collected, and they were placed in the centre. This was one of the results of this event. And it was perhaps in order to prevent BH Army members from killing Croats, and partly, it was in order to protect ourselves, protect themselves and to protect those people among them because unfortunately no one could be a guarantee for anyone in that town any more, and life unfortunately was worth very little. Among those detainees, naturally at the very beginning, there were probably or rather I am sure that there were people who could not be included in the groups that I have mentioned. So people who were under 18 years of age or people who were over 65 years of age and so on. So sometime at the beginning of the conflict, that was the first time I heard about people being detained. The first time I heard about people being detained was at the meeting I mentioned with Halilovic when he accused Petkovic and said that we had detained certain people. That was on the 4th of May. After that, I know for sure that all these people were released because that had been agreed at the meeting. That was one of the issues that had been agreed on at the meeting. After this open conflict that I have been speaking about, the situation in the town was such that it was impossible to get information about this or to find out about how events were being influenced. So there was an open conflict which was taking place on a daily basis in the town itself. The medical services were making a great effort in order to treat all those who had been wounded, and at that time, I would say that this was a priority for us. Immediately after that period of time, I think that was somewhere in the middle of July, because of a trip I had arranged for Canada earlier on, I was absent. I think I wasn't in Mostar for about 20 or 25 days. When I returned, I think that was in mid-July, in the meantime the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO had unfortunately escalated. Then I heard from my colleagues, other doctors, about the existence of the -- of this detention centre. They told me that, that they were involved in looking after all -- of all the detainees who needed medical care. They also told me that they looked after them every day. I made a decision -- the following decision. I thought that one could not deny the existence of the centre, if the centre did exist, as it did, and I invited the member of the Helsinki watch for the protection of human rights from Zagreb, professor Slobodan Lang, and together with him, I went to the Heliodrom. I must admit that my first meeting with Heliodrom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we could get some foundation of time as to when this visit to the Heliodrom was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Witness, would you please tell us about the time when you visited Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't. I can't remember the date. But I know that it must have been in mid-July, but I can't say that with certainty. But I can check that. So the Heliodrom left a strong impact on me and when we got there, somebody approached me, one of the people who were there, and told me that there were a number of people detained there. I asked him how many. And he said several thousand. I was very concerned with the overall situation regarding the war, the battle front, and when I saw this detention centre and when it had occurred to me that a number of such detention centres existed all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Croats were detained and that in these centres, people perished in huge numbers, after that, together with Slobodan Lang, I drafted a certain plan as to what we should do, as doctors. We made contact with the doctors who were in charge in that area, and we talked to them. Secondly, the International Red Cross had already been aware of that and we also talked to them. We decided to become active in order to prevent possible suffering of those people, and in order to provide the international organisations with a better insight into the situation, with a view to preventing any large-scale suffering. During the next few days, our doctors supervised the situation in this detention centre. However, we decided to establish a team of doctors outside the centre. I was one of the members of that team. We also appointed the leader of that team, that was Dr. Curic a specialist in infectious diseases. We also had a specialist in general medicine, Dr. Sandrka. Dr. Lang was also a member of that team and also one of his assistants, Mr. Culo. As a result of the work of that team, we accomplished the following: We established a medical team within the detention centre. We established a small department, a small ward, where all those who needed help in the detention centre would be treated. We assigned a place and a person in charge of medicines and logistics, which had to do with medicine. So we established a little storage of medicines. We also assigned an ambulance vehicle, which was dedicated for the needs of the detention centre. All the people who were there and who required medical treatment would, from then on, be transported to the hospital where they were treated. So in a nutshell, what was our goal and what we achieved? We wanted to prevent individual and large-scale suffering of the people in the detention centre. Secondly, we wanted to treat all those who needed medical care. And thirdly, we wanted to prevent the breakout of epidemics, of any contagious disease. Fourthly, we wanted to cooperate, as much as we could, with international organisations. We achieved the following. All those who required medical assistance indeed received it. All those who needed to be referred to the hospital were sent to the hospital and treated there. We enabled Dr. Mirsad Stanjak who was also a detainee in the detention centre, to have supervision of all that work with in the detention centre and to communicate with whoever visited the centre. We partly succeeded in providing for an efficient communication with international organisations because the food that was brought for the detainees was in short supply, and did not meet their needs. As for other structures are concerned, primarily the structures within the HVO, we succeeded in preventing, i.e., reducing, any -- if there was any mistreatment of the people there, and one other thing that we managed to succeed in was to prevent a large-scale suffering. And finally, I would like to say that the detention centre for us was unfortunately one of the non-desired outcomes, that we did not expect, and that is why our knowledge as to how we should treat that centre, what to do, what the role of the Red Cross was, in terms of that centre, so at the beginning, our knowledge was really modest in that respect. However, despite all the sufferings of the people who were detained and by the sheer fact that they were detained they suffered, so despite all that, we managed to achieve most of our objectives. So much for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Bagaric. Can you tell us something that my learned colleague is also going to ask you about and I don't want to waste any time, you said that Dr. Lang came as a member of the Helsinki watch. Some witnesses said here in this courtroom that they had another function?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What function, I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever a political function in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm sorry for interrupting. I believe that this is a very unusual situation for you, but whenever I deem it necessary to interrupt you, I will. Don't please hold it against me. So let's go back to Dr. Lang, the Croatian Helsinki watch was a non-governmental organisation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here in this courtroom, we heard testimony that he arrived as an adviser to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is true, then -- Tudjman -- but at the time, Dr. Lang did not have any political or any other role. He was just a professor of public health in the -- at the Andrija Stampar school in Zagreb and he was a member of the Helsinki watch of Zagreb and before that, and at the time, and today, he has had a lot of experience with humanitarian aid, and providing humanitarian help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may be asking you some unusual -- some strange questions but let me explain why I'm doing that. Was he prone to drinking? Did he drink alcohol, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time with Dr. Lang. I never saw the man having as much as a glass of beer, let alone wine or spirits, and I claim here before you that nobody could ever see him drunk because, I don't know whether I'm allowed to say this here, but I shall say it, because he is on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. medication which do not go well with alcohol. And he is really not prone to alcohol. And I never saw him drinking. So this is a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a special position or attitude towards other people who were not Croats, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, Slobodan Lang? He has his position on everything, I should think so. I believe that he has a position on -- and attitude towards all nations, but his general position is that all people are equal, and that all people deserve help if they need help, and in his work, he has demonstrated that, and I can give you several examples for that if the Honourable Court will allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It would be a waste of time. I just would like to show you Exhibit D1/382, page 33, a short question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, if I may, Your Honours, this is a gift which I have carried on me around my neck, but today I'm wearing a tie so I can't do that today. This is what Slobodan Lang gave me. This depicts three symbols, three large religions as a sign of universality which does not exclude any religious, either Jewish, Islam, or Catholic. I'm a person who is trying to be a good Catholic. I'm also entitled to wear this around my neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've asked for Exhibit D1/382. And also, Madam Registrar, can you also prepare D1/348 and D1/347 and 372? And this will be the basis for my last set of questions. We are going to show you these documents and we are drawing to the end of this examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, another unusual question: Do you know what is Dr. Lang's either nationality or religion? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have the right to talk about Dr. Lang, because of what I said and what I can confirm, I don't see the need to talk any longer about this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just tell you that somebody in this courtroom said that Dr. Lang had a very negative position about Muslims. So this is not by chance that I'm asking you what is his religion or what is his nationality. And this exhibit, 1/382?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President again as I have several times in the last few sessions, I object to these argumentative questions. That question that was just put to the witness had no more -- only for the effect of educating the witness and talking the witness into answer that counsel wanted. I object to that form of question. It's happened repeatedly now. And we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just ask a simple question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. I'm not trying to lead this witness. This witness cannot be led anywhere. This witness is testifying the way he wants to testify. He can not be led into saying anything by anybody. But I think that this is a very important question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind, I know that you're avoiding any mention of anybody's religion or nationality but still, can you tell us if you ever noticed that Dr. Lang would have a negative attitude towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to thank Mr. Scott for saying -- for suggesting that I may be saying what somebody else wants me to say. But rest assured, Mr. Scott, and Your Honours, that I will say only what I know, what is the truth and I will say that everywhere and at all times. Dr. Lang is a person who spent time before the war with miners from Trepca, and they are all Albanians, all Muslims. He spent sometime with them under the ground, in the mines, and he went on strike, on hunger strike, with them, because they were persecuted by the Serbs. That was before the war. During the war, Dr. Lang helped everybody, after the war, during the Kosovo crisis, Dr. Lang went to Kosovo. Dr. Lang is a universal person when it comes to his attitude towards religion. So it is not my place to say anything about his family tree or ancestry and I don't want to comment on that, but one thing I can say for sure, that never ever did I hear from that man a word about anybody in any situation at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you have documents in front of you. Can you please give us your comments and we shall close with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I can see several papers, documents talking about my experience during my work, during the war. Some of them also concern Dr. Lang. For example I'm holding in my hand document D1/347. That is an article which has been published by Richard Horton the editor-in-chief of Lancet, and Lancet is one of the leading scientific, I apologise for telling you this I'm sure you know but it is one of the leading scientific papers and on the basis of our experience, he published a -- something about our attempts to mitigate the suffering of our enemies at the time, during the war. But also our sufferings, the suffering of all of us, to my mind. He mentions in this article that this is something that the world should look up to, that the world should follow -- follow in our foot steps because it shows a wonderful attitude towards the humanitarian aid and it shows wonderful efficiency of the medical service during the war. So on the same subject, I spoke in Montreal, the topic was the consequences of war on people, hospitals and medical personnel from the public health respective view. As a result of that speech, the article that I'm holding in my hand, D1/347, and especially article D1/382, which was presented by Slobodan Lang and myself in Strasbourg on the conference on medicine and human rights. So these are the attempts in order to advance the international humanitarian law, based on our experience. Among the proposals which are listed here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I would like to speed you up a little because the time is constrained. Just a short commentary because everybody can read the document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We proposed setting up of the so-called global hospital. We proposed some improvements with regard to detention centres. And we touched upon many other subjects. At a conference in Canada, this knowledge was also used and the whole conference wanted to use our experience in order to come to the new knowledge on the prevention of war, prevention on hate and on how to be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm again interrupting you. I want your comment on 1/348 and 1/372, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: D1/348 is an overview of the sufferings of Croats in central Bosnia, in the Neretva valley. It's just an overview of all the sufferings. D1/372 is relative to an issue that I can talk about here, because I want this to be heard. I want this to be known. This is relative to the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state has survived. That is my testimony. That is something that I have the need to tell you here, as the witness of that time. So it has survived primarily as the result of the influence of the international community, and to a large extent, as the result of the contribution of the people to which I belong. In a lecture that I delivered in Harvard I said that the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina is due much more to the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina than to any other people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I explained that by the fact that we Croats were the first ones to vote for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at our referendum, we voted for an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council was the first established defence unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we have heard all those evidence already. I hope you could be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, let me finish. I understand you for warning me. Thank you for your warning. Document 1/372 demonstrates Croatian isolated zones during the war in Bosnia, besides the Croatian Defence Council and the BH Army, and huge aid from Croatia, in terms of medical assistance and receipt of Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees, these Croat enclaves remained until the end of the war as the connecting tissue of the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and owing to them, the Dayton Accords could be signed, they were preceded by the Washington Agreements and the condition of those were cantons, some of which were to be mixed. So the fighting of the Croats in central Bosnia and Herzegovina was the foundation for resolving the conflict between Muslims and Croats, i.e., for creating a federation and later on, the peace accords in -- for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would conclude with that unless --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have another question, I apologise, Dr. Bagaric, there are rules that we have to adhere to and we have to respect this court. Did you ever see Dr. Lang -- so the first question is do you know Mr. Naletilic personally?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean do I know him? Well, at the moment I can assume who Mr. Naletilic is because among other things, I saw certain photographs when he was arrested, and out of the two or three people sitting here, I can guess who he is but I don't know him personally, I don't know Mr. Naletilic personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen or did Mr. Lang tell you about this or were you present, have you seen Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Lang visiting the Heliodrom together?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, and Mr. Lang never mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times did Dr. Lang go to the Heliodrom? Were you always with him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times Lang was at the Heliodrom but I do know that I never heard a comment from him about having seen this person or that person or having been with this person or that person and certainly not with Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all, Your Honours. I have no further questions. I thank you, Mr. Bagaric, for your patience. The Prosecutor will now cross-examine you. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Scott? Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll just note for the record, Your Honour, that Mr. Krsnik's direct examination took just slightly under four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we have calculated the time spent for Mr. Krsnik but any way, thank you very much to remind me of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that fact is simply not correct. I can't understand how Mr. Scott calculated the time, four hours. Altogether, I can tell you precisely, one hour and 15 minutes, two hours, not even three hours. Not even three hours. I really don't see how this was calculated. Maybe we should use a stop watch to calculate it. I really don't understand how the time is being calculated. Maybe some other sort of time is being calculated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to understand that the Registrar also calculates the time you used for the direct examination. I think both parties have to trust the calculation made by the Registrar. According to her calculation, it's about four hours. Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the latter part of November, 1993, was there anyone who was filled the position that might be called the minister, the HVO Minister of Health or some such -- that may mot be the exact title. Please understand I'm not asking you specific words but was there someone who filled a position that was something like the HVO or Herceg-Bosna Minister of Health? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the position of the director of the health department, not a minister, but I think that at that time it was called a subdepartment for health. It was a part of the government, of the civil structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the head of the health department as you described it, as of mid-November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A friend of mine, whose name is Ivan Sarac and he too contributed to a great extent and helped us implement what we did in the course of the war, helped us to provide health care to all those who needed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you continue to be the assistant, essentially the assistant Minister of Defence for medicine, for medical services or health? How long did you continue in that position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, we could say, a coordinator of the main medical headquarters, directly prior to the formation, not of that ministry but of the department, of the Defence department, and I think that this was up until, I think, the Defence department was formed -- I think it was in August. I can't be exact. August, 1992. I was the assistant of the chief of the Defence department for health. That's what it was called. And I had this -- held this post from that date right up until the Dayton agreement, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for date purposes, perhaps you can assist the Chamber, when you say the Dayton agreement, so what date was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date of the Dayton agreement, but I don't know the exact date but it was in 1995, I think it was -- well, I don't know exactly. Perhaps the first half of 1995. I don't know. I can't remember. That's when the peace agreement was concluded in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it can we understand, and most importantly can the Judges, sir, understand that throughout the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims or for that matter all of 1993, all of 1994, you were the most senior HVO official, if you will, dedicated or having the task of health services; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an HVO officer, or rather the commander of the health service of the -- the commander of the so-called war health, the war component, and that related to the organisation of health in units, the organisation of war hospitals, and during that period, that was the role I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question, then. Throughout -- I'll go back to the late 1992 just to be clear. Throughout the second half of approximately of 1992, all of 1993, and all of 1994, you were the most senior health and medical-related official or officer in the HVO or the government of Herceg-Bosna, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had medical --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had a medical or health-related function more senior to you in either the HVO or the government of either respectively the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or later the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna? Who had a more senior position than you in those areas?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me and if you don't interrupt me, I will answer your question. With regard to the organisation of military health, health that was related to units, no one was more senior than I was, no one. When we are talking about civil health, that's a different segment and was responsible for the medical centres which weren't in the war zone. And that part, I don't know, it's part of the government, whatever you call it, the government of Herceg-Bosna. I wasn't in the government. I was a member of the -- within the Ministry of Defence I was an assistant to the minister of defence, and I was the assistant for health. No one of the doctors was above me, no one -- I was under no one's orders in that segment of the health service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please assist the Chamber with saying who then was the mast senior health or medicine-related official on the government side, as you just described it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the so-called subdepartment for health, whom I have already mentioned. He was a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us his name again, just so it's clear, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ivan Saric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the wartime, we can all understand that under wartime conditions, situations in a field hospital could be clearly quite severe and unpleasant. The situation in the West Mostar hospital was terrible, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what terrible means?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir, you tell me. What were the conditions then? Was it pleasant? Did you have all the supplies you needed? Was it a pleasant place to work or was it a very unpleasant and terrible situation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question related to the west part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The west side hospital, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not pleasant to work anywhere during a war. We didn't have enough doctors. There was a shortage of equipment. And medical supplies were lacking too. But as I said, compared with the east side of Mostar, we were in a good situation. But when you compare it with the east side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's my next question, sir. Isn't it true that, as terrible as conditions may have been in the west side hospital, conditions in the hospital in East Mostar were far worse in every respect? Weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could have the usher please show you Exhibit D1/376. I may have it wrong. Excuse me. I may have -- excuse me, Mr. Usher, I may have the wrong number. Sorry, give me one moment, please. My apology. I'm sorry, it's 354, if you could show the witness, please, Exhibit D1/354. Mr. Usher if you could assist us, please, by putting the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the date of this document that you've told us you prepared is the 14th of April, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was substantially before any major armed conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before any major conflict, in Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you assist us, please, with why the name of the hospital as reflected in the first sentence under the title or section heading called, "Communication". It says this: "A meeting of physicians, Croats and Muslims, service heads, and the command of the HVO regional war hospital, Mostar." Why was it the HVO regional war hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's what its name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, why wasn't it just simply called the Mostar regional hospital? What was the significance of claiming that it was an HVO hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the decision on naming that hospital was brought by the municipal council of the town of Mostar, at a time when it had its government, it had its Commander of Defence, and that was a time when I think -- I think Jasmin Jaganjac, who at the time was the commander of the Defence of the town and was later an officer in the BH Army, he personally, and a representative of the municipal council, named that hospital and decided that it should be a war hospital, from the time of the conflict with the Serbs. That was from the time of the conflict with the Serbs, so at an earlier date, a date prior to this date, when this document was written, this hospital was already called a war hospital because a decision had already been made to that effect, and primarily, I said this on several times, because of the war situation, because it was surrounded. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, sir, that from the spring of 1992, and continuing through to April of 1993 and thereafter, Mostar, the city of Mostar, and its government, was controlled by the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Mostar, I think it was in 1992, maybe in September. What happened in Mostar before that date, before that time, I know what the situation was with the organisation of health, but for me to talk to you about who had authority, power, in Mostar after the first free elections, well, I really can't do that but the results of the free elections in Mostar defined the power structure in Mostar, as is the case everywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From September 1992, sir, when you arrived there, continuing to April, 1993, and thereafter, the HVO controlled the government of Mostar and the infrastructure in Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO, has both a military and a civil structure. And a decision was taken about this just before the conflict, and during the conflict, or rather during the Serbian aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'll repeat this: Up until the war with the Serbs, the authorities functioned like authorities everywhere in the world, in Mostar. The conflict with the Serbs, or rather the Serbian aggression and the formation of the HVO, well, if we are talking about the military component in the town, it was under -- the town was under the command of the HVO, and the HVO liberated the town from the Serbs, too, but with regard to this question, as to who was in command of the town and certain other structures, I really don't know. I just didn't deal with that. It was not a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your position, then, sir, before this Chamber, that, for instance, in June and July of 1993, then, are you telling this Chamber the Muslims had just as much control in the government of West Mostar and most of Mostar, as the Croats did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June and July, 1993, no one had control over anything, because it was war. So in June and July, 1993, it was a time of war. So there was part of the town which was under HVO control and there was part of the town which was under the BH Army, under the control of the BH Army. I don't understand what you want to ask me, what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Herceg-Bosna was created, sir, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mostar was declared the capital of Herceg-Bosna, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this declaration was ever made, or in fact I don't know, but I think that the formation of Herceg-Bosna didn't have as its objective the declaration of a capital, and the declaration of Herceg-Bosna some sort of creation, some sort of structure, because Herceg-Bosna during the war and after the war, right up until the signing of the peace agreement or let's say up until the time when the government of Herceg-Bosna ceased to function, it was a territorial unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that in one of its founding documents, it says that the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina is respected. So in all the documents that I saw then, in this document here too, the document that you gave me, it says the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the top, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the Defence department. So it was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which still hadn't fell into the hands of the Serbs. So I really don't know anything about the capital. I really know nothing about Mostar as the capital. I apologise. I really don't know how to it address you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
