utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna was a government, was it not, sir, with a president, a legislature, judges, a military, postal service, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and it was a government, sir, with all the characteristics of a government that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. most of us would recognise as a government, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. When someone asked me, when the Prosecutor asks me, whether that was correct, do I always have to say either yes or no or can I provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course, you could explain your views on this subject. But first, you have to -- if possible, you have to answer yes or no to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I would like to say the following. To answer such a question by saying yes or no, well, such -- providing such answers could be used to confirm what someone wants to hear, whether it's the Defence or the Prosecution. So in such matters, I would really like to ask you not to be compelled to answer by saying yes or no. So the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, later on it was never territorially defined. It was never a separated territory. It was never separated from Bosnia-Herzegovina. You asked me whether there was a government there. Well, of course. There was a government in order to introduce order and defend the territory. It's not possible to defend territory if there is no order in existence. It was a government but it wasn't a government which compromised Bosnia and Herzegovina or rather which intended -- which wanted to separate from Bosnia and Herzegovina and later on to ask for international recognition of some kind, et cetera, et cetera. So, that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The government of Herceg-Bosna that you've just identified was controlled by the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The HVO was under the control of the legitimate representatives of the government from the first multi-party elections. So it is true that the HVO was under the control of the official representatives of people from certain territory. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the President of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was a Bosnian Croat named Mate Boban, correct? Is that a difficult question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, it's a very difficult question, why? [Interpretation] I'll try and explain this to you. Mate Boban, he was firstly a member of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he was a colleague of mine in parliament. Therefore, with the establishment of the HVO or rather the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and of the HVO et cetera, Mate Boban as a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina or rather a representative of the people, a legitimate representative, he carried out these functions, he carried out the functions of the duties of president, or rather of chief or I don't know, in that territory. So to that extent, my answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the President of the HVO government was a man named Jadranko Prlic, who was also a Bosnian Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see that I haven't been raising any objections but the Prosecutor is always allowing himself to do things that he shouldn't be allowed to do. I respect all of your decisions. You can see what Mr. Bagaric's testimony related to. I don't know what these political questions are about, about the HZ HB, but that was not something that I addressed in my direct examination, and the gentleman didn't come here to testify about these facts and I didn't question him about them either. And I would like to repeat, Your Honours, and this is something I would like to it announce, I think that I'm going to modify my form of examination because I don't want the cross-examination to be taken -- made use of, one knows very well what the purpose of cross-examination is. I have analysed all the witnesses, just a moment ago, and the Prosecutor or the OTP, they have their investigation teams and they have had seven years to carry out their investigations and this is not something that should be done during cross-examination under the cover of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, according to your 65 ter filings, we understand this witness is only going to testify about war hospital and all those matters related. But during your direct examinations, you asked very extensive questions which out of the scope of that 65 ter filings. In this aspect, I think the Prosecution is entitled to ask all those related questions, which, as the witness said himself, Mr. Mate Boban worked with him in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honours. There was one question at the beginning to which my learned friend objected, when we started talking about the parliament of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina he objected immediately and after that I stopped talking about politics. All the other questions were about the war hospital, the organisation of health care and so on and so forth. And now he is using the same questions that he objected to during my examination-in-chief. So very often, my learned friend contradicts himself and he always interprets things the way he chooses to interpret them and he does not allow the other side, i.e. the defence to interpret things their way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to answer that question, I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we just heard that the witness would like to answer this question, and we'll break now and after the break, we will hear the answer from this witness. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I please ask you a favour? Actually can I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it is not through fault of yours or mine, I have been here for quite a long time. Is there any way, I'm appealing to Mr. Prosecutor, is there anyway that my testimony could be finished today? Otherwise, I have to stay for another weekend, and this would very much dictate the way I answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bagaric, before starting this hearing, this Trial Chamber has done its utmost to try to find a courtroom and proper time to finish your testimony today. But all our efforts have failed. So I'm afraid that you have to stay here during the weekend. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. So I apologise. Can I ask the Prosecutor to repeat the question? And I would also kindly ask him to understand me and try to do his best so I don't have to stay here over the weekend, I can even promise that I will be very short, up to the point, as long as I can go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question, sir, was is it not true, sir, that Jadranko Prlic was the President of the HVO government and a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he is a Croat, and I don't know whether he was the President of the government all the time. However, one way to answer this question is yes, but this is not true, because when I say yes, then it is a generally known thing that Jadranko Prlic did discharge the duties mentioned by the Prosecutor but the truth is a much broader thing and it requires a certain explanation. The truth is, the whole information and the whole information is as follows: Jadranko Prlic was the Prime Minister of one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, during which we defended ourselves from Serbia and during all this time belonged to Bosnia and Herzegovina and which after the war was incorporated, together with Republika Srpska, together with the areas controlled by the BH Army, into Bosnia and Herzegovina. This would be a much better answer, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jadran Topic was the Mayor of Mostar and the HVO President of Mostar, a Bosnian Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live during the war, sir, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over Bosnia and Herzegovina, in different places in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was in Posavina, I was in central Bosnia. I was in the area of my native Tomislavgrad, where I have my house. I also was in Mostar for a little while. I was even stationed in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you give us an idea a sir, again, of where you spent most of your time in 1993, in terms of where you stayed, where you had your residence, when you were not working?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always worked. There was no single day when I didn't work. So my family house is in Tomislavgrad municipality but that is where I spent the least time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the most time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No particular village, city or municipality? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been Tomislavgrad. I think I spent most time in Tomislavgrad, if I measured the time, but I would have to do a little research in order to be able to tell you that. I can't tell you with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you in the last few moments was where you lived and now I'm asking you separate question: Where was your principal office or place of work during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's different question and I thank you for it. We established the medical headquarters in 1992 in Tomislavgrad. Why? Because Tomislavgrad is in the area between Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a part which is equally -- at an equal distance from all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the office throughout the war remained there with the personnel that we had and then, from late 1992, I spent some time in Mostar, and after that, some time in Posusje. So I was in different places and my office was partly throughout the war was in Tomislavgrad, and the second part of my office was for a while in Mostar and later on in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said you would try to give us short, responsive answers. Listen to my question, please. Specifically directed to 1993. I did not ask you about why it was put in Grude or why or anything about 1992. Where was your principal office or place of work during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you before that and you didn't answer me. Are you going to ask me short questions so that you can let me go home? If you want to do that, then my answers will be brief. If not, then I really have all the time in the world. I will be more specific and I will give you more complete information. That may be of some use to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have no intentions of negotiating with you about my cross-examination, my question to you and the question pending is where was your principal office or place of work during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, my place of work, my office, was in Mostar, throughout 1993 and if you wish to know, I never had an office in Grude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can the Judges understand, some of the important aspects of this case, that throughout most of 1993, you actually worked in the city of Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that everybody can understand, not just the Honourable Court. In 1993, I was in Mostar, that is my office was there, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I did not sit there all the time, because my area of authority was not only Mostar but everywhere where the HVO was, and that was the entire area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wherever there were Croats. So I travelled a lot, all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, even in that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that is the reason for the questions which I'm putting to you which are very simple so that the Judges can understand the basis of your knowledge about various things that you've talked to us about. So I'm trying to establish where you were and for how long. Now, did you spend most of your time actually working in west -- West Mostar, or were you equally out and about all parts of Herzegovina during 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of my working hours, I spent in Mostar. I mentioned that I was in Canada for some 20 days during that time. I must have been elsewhere during that time but my office, my workplace, the workplace of my colleagues who were in charge of the medical corps of the HVO, was in Mostar. And now, when I see where you are headed, then, yes, the answer is I spent most of the time in Mostar and my office was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the approximate time period when you were in Canada? I know it's a long time ago but your best estimate of the beginning date and when you returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I left for Canada -- just a moment -- in the second half of June, and I returned -- just a moment, please. No. Let me correct myself. I think it was earlier that I left, and I returned before the 20th of June. So this was between the end of May and the 20th of June when I believe I returned. I have to try and remember that in comparison with some other dates and events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, during that period of time, you have no firsthand knowledge of anything that happened in Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. I knew what I could know. I had regular contacts with the doctors who were in Mostar and I had information that they had, and that was available to them, the information that was relevant, and which was pertinent to the functioning of the medical care of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the information you had about any event in Mostar during that time was entirely hearsay, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those 20 days when I was not in Mostar, I could not leave my clone there. So during those 20 days, I received information from other people, because I was not physically there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reports, and they can be placed in front of you, if it would help you sir and I leave it to you, the reports that were marked as D1/359 and D1/381, the reports that were about the time when you were talking about the events around Jablanica and Sovici Doljani which Judge Clark asked you about, if you recall, in looking at those reports on Wednesday, or Tuesday, it was, excuse me, those reports themselves don't say anything about what happened in Sovici-Doljani, what you saw, or any conclusions that you reached, do they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. These reports clearly show that the Muslim side achieved all of their goals and that we didn't. We did not get to where we were supposed to go, where we had to do, and the Muslim side on the other hand, did. I repeat once again: I'm here to testify as to what I saw there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I put it to you that the reports talk about the process that you told about, no question about that, they talk about meetings, leading up to a mission, if you want to call it that, to Sovici-Doljani, which happened just finally on -- around the 4th of May, the day before the report was written but neither of those reports, sir, provide the Chamber with any information about the actual mission or activities or assessment made in Sovici or Doljani, do they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. It is not correct that there is no information about that, because as far as I remember, both reports emphasised that there was a visit to Sovici and Doljani because amongst other things, one report says that a convoy that was supposed to go in a different direction, that it had to wait at the checkpoint for us to return from Sovici and Doljani, those of us who had been there. So it says here that the visit did take place and this is also to be found in the report. The report says that the visit did take place and it also says in the report that the representatives of the BH Army achieved their goal and their goal, their objective, was to visit precisely these two places, and I was personally a member of the delegation which visited these two places, on top of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the book that is called the "Angel of Mostar" which is D1/383, is it your understanding that that book was written by this woman, Sally Baker?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, according to information available to all the readers, whether a book has been written by somebody or not, this can only be concluded from the signature of the author. This book has been signed by Sally Baker. I don't have any reason whatsoever to doubt that. Whether she had help, I don't know, but the main thoughts in that book are the thoughts of Mrs. Sally Baker, and I witnessed some of the events that she describes in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Mrs. Baker herself to gave herself the title, "The Angel of Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who has given the book this title, "The Angel of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But however that title came about, whatever else the book may be about, Sally Baker was helping the Muslims in East Mostar, and that's what she became known for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. It's just partly correct. She helped Croats as well, Croats on the western side of Mostar, and also Croats in central Bosnia, who were -- and Muslims on the eastern side of Mostar. So this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the people killed on the 9th of May, 1993, as I understand it, sir, if you know, most of the attack, whoever started it, and let me understand I'm not suggesting who started it at the moment, I don't want to get bogged down in that, but much of the fighting was in the early morning hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which people do you refer to as to people who were killed on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any people, sir, on the 9th of May, 1993, killed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What about them is your question to me? That I haven't already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. My question to you, sir, was, is it true that much of the fighting that broke out in Mostar on the 9th of May, was in the early morning hours, had nothing to do with who was killed, I simply asked you the time of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about victims, these victims were falling all day long so I was talking about the total number of victims throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not understand my question? My question is: Is it true that much of the fighting took place in the early morning hours of the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've been listening very carefully and I really don't know what has entered -- what has been entered in the transcript. The Prosecutor asked whether these victims fell during the early hours of the morning, and the witness replied throughout the day. And then the Prosecutor says this is not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you may ask a simple question, when do you believe -- when do you believe the fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With all respect, Your Honour, that's not my question. My question is and it's very simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that much of the fighting in Mostar started in the early morning hours of the 9th of May? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a simple answer. I don't know when most of the fighting took place, as you put it. I was talking about victims. I did not say anything about the development of the war events, with the war operations, in which I did not take place, I was not a soldier, neither am I able to assess them or to be the judge of their development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know, you didn't see the unfortunately and we can all agree that what happened was tragic on all sides, but you were not present where the bodies fell, so when you talk about 100, approximately 100 persons being either killed or seriously wounded, by shots to the head, you did not see these bodies in place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the answer, and that was that I don't understand fighting as fighting. I don't know when fightings take place or don't take place. As far as the victims, the dead and the injured are concerned, I said that on that day, there were a lot of casualties, a lot of injured. That with my own two eyes I saw a number of ambulance vehicles which brought the injured to the hospital. These people were treated. Some of them survived the treatment, some of them died. Many people were killed on that day. And this is all I said. And of course I saw patients in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw these people, that were seriously wounded or unfortunately perhaps bodies, primarily or entirely at the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not bodies that were brought to the hospital but the wounded. I'm talking about the wounded, those who were alive when they were brought. So I could not see -- obviously I couldn't see them all. Some of these people died of their wounds and some survived. So I'm talking about these people, those that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Defence counsel was very specific with you and you gave a very specific answer that you estimated that approximately 100 people that day were either killed or seriously wounded by shots directly to the head. Now, is that your testimony or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on that day, there were about 100 victims, either injured or killed. If I said that every -- and each and every one of them was shot straight into the head, then I was wrong. I expressed myself wrongly. I said that according to what I saw and what I heard from the people down there, a number of people were shot either in the head or in the neck, and that after that, I issued a recommendation that all the soldiers were to wear a helmet, and I myself started wearing a helmet from that day on, and some of my colleagues laughed at me behind my back and they said I got scared. But yes, I did, because I knew that I could get shot even me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these approximate 100 victims, can you tell us again, please or clarify, were they mostly civilians or were they mostly soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you at this moment who they were, but I know for sure there were both civilians and soldiers. Unfortunately, I cannot answer your question with precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, wouldn't it be -- and again unfortunately, would it be the case, when fighting occurred when people were in their homes and flats, and when people went to their windows to see what was going on, trying to protect themselves but peek out over a window or behind a door, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that many of the wounds or injuries would be to the head? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question is a matter of speculation. I think that it's clear that the witness saw these bodies in the hospital and to reply to all these questions, it would be necessary to speculate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Krsnik. Mr. Scott, move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move on but we will also object, it's also further speculation of any conclusions that the Defence would draw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times, sir, from approximately May of 1993, until November, 1993, did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer allow my colleague to give testimony and to come to conclusions which then enter the transcript when the witness quite clearly told me he didn't know what people were -- what sort of weapons caused the shots to the head. He said this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I did not see this question, at least, in the transcript. Well, let us hear the whole question from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, my question was moving on and I won't belabour the last points further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was, starting in approximately June of 1993, sir, and continuing until the end of 1993, can you give the Judges to your best estimate of how many times you were actually physically present at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I visited the Heliodrom, at the time I assumed that I had been there, so on that occasion, I personally went to the Heliodrom only once, but my colleagues, doctors who were under me and whom I held accountable, they were in constant contact with the Heliodrom, or they were at the Heliodrom in person. A group of medical personnel was present at the Heliodrom all the time. I also mentioned the detained doctor who was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... try to move along so I'm going to try to move along. Your answer is that during that time period from June to December, 1993, you were at the Heliodrom yourself one time. Now, let me ask you about the HVO prison camp at Ljubuski. How many times were you physically at the prison camp at Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Ljubuski detention centre is concerned, well, I've never heard about it, I've never heard about a detention centre in Ljubuski. I was never there. But if it's correct to say that such a centre did exist, then I am sure that the health care there was provided by the doctors --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... how many times were at the fast I will the at Gabela?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be fair to say the military prison centre in Ljubuski. The Prosecutor is using his own term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is there any difference about this term?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know of any difference, Your Honour, a place in Ljubuski administered by the HVO where people were held against their will. How about that for a definition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, whatever terms you use, so long as it could get cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever at a facility, sir, administered by the HVO in the area of the city or town of Ljubuski where Muslim prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer is no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say no, but I said that I -- that at this moment I really don't know whether such a centre existed but if it did, I most certainly was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever present physically personally present at an HVO facility where Muslim prisoners were held in the vicinity of Gabela?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I would like certain things to be clear in this transcript. I brought this witness here for your sake, Your Honours, in order to provide you with an entire picture of health care in Mostar. This is what we are all interested. I could have asked four questions and concluded my examination. When I said that there was a difference with regard to the terms, that's true. But I said a military investigation prison. That is the official name of that prison in Ljubuski. And it's a term used by the Prosecutor with his witnesses. And thus he is confusing the witness because when he says a detention centre, well maybe there was another detention centre in Ljubuski. There was a military investigation prison and people went there in accordance with the decisions of the military investigating judge and I think that this is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, use the term used by the Defence counsel. Try to come across this idea to the witness. Let's see what is the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever at any time between June and the end of December of 1993 at the military investigative prison at Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever at any sort of HVO prison or detention facility in the vicinity of Gabela during that same time period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever present yourself at an HVO detention facility, either called or at the vicinity of the Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question -- if you want me to say that I wasn't there because I didn't care, if that's what you're aiming at with your question, then I will to provide more extensive answers to all these questions, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that's not my question. If you would please, I invite you with all respects, Mr. President, not to speculate about what my question means or where it leads, just answer the question, if you would, please, that I ask you. My question was not to suggest whether you cared or not cared. The question is simple. From June of 1993 to the end of December, 1993, were you ever physically present at an HVO detention facility at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dretelj, as in all other detention centres, there was a medical service which had been established, as I have said, and there were people who were responsible for it at its head and they were under me. I was never there personally, but they were there and they provided those people with health care, and I was in regular contact with them, and there were written reports which were also provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that brings me in fact directly to the question I was going to ask you: In the HVO structure, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you understand the concept of military command, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do but I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your boss, sir? Who did you take direction from? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just asked you in what sense do you mean "boss"? In a professional sense? Or does this refer to the structure of the Ministry of Defence of which I was a part or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were the assistant Minister of Defence for health or health services, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the structure of the Ministry of Defence, my place within that ministry, as you said, I was the assistant of the Minister of Defence. So that means that the Minister of Defence, within those structures was my superior. But if we are talking in professional terms, unfortunately, or fortunately perhaps, no one was above me. I did not have a superior because I was the highest ranking commander for health in the HVO, if we are talking about the organisation of the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about the structure of the HVO Ministry of Defence, sir. So your superior was the Minister of Defence, who during the time, June of 1993, until the latter part of 1993, was Bruno Stojic, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. For sometime, Bruno Stojic was my superior but Perica Jukic was also my superior for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir in late, in very late, I agree with you, perhaps we -- can we agree that from perhaps late November, 1993, until the end of the year, Mr. Jukic was your superior? Prior to that, it was Bruno Stojic, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have really told you very clearly in my answer what the case was. I have answered the question. I was absolutely precise, as I promised to be, and I corrected the Prosecutor, and said that, yes, for a certain period of time, but for another period of time, I don't know for how long, my superior was Perica Jukic. I have already answered that question. I do not understand why is it necessary once I have provided an answer to ask me the question again? What is the importance of this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reporting mechanism, sir, to either Mr. Stojic or to Mr. Jukic? Did you make a weekly -- a daily report, a weekly report? What sort of regular reporting did you provide to the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had meetings which were held every week. The reports that you are referring to, I really don't remember how I submitted such reports, but what I do know for a fact is that if we are talking about the organisation of health care in wartime, and how this health care is provided, I had a significant level of independence and no one --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. You had a superior who was the Minister of Defence. What regular reports did you make to him? If any? If you made no reports you can say you made no reports.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you. We had occasional meetings at which we reported on the situation in the areas of various individuals for which various individuals were responsible. I then spoke about the problems of the -- of health care, of the health service and there were written reports as I have already said, but I do not know how often we submitted such reports, but they did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were your immediate subordinates, sir, the people who reported directly to you as their superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we talking about the profession, about medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the HVO Ministry of Defence sir and the people in that structure who were your direct subordinates.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question now. The chiefs of the -- the heads of departments and sections of the main medical headquarters were my subordinates. That's the first thing. And then after the restructuring took place, the chief of the health administration was my subordinate, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heads of individual departments within that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now a few minutes ago you were telling us -- I was asking you questions about some of the HVO detention facilities. Was it your position that there was at least one medical officer at each of those facilities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. And that doesn't mean either yes or no. What I said was that in all those centres you ever been talking about, we organised health care in all of those centres, and the doctors and other medical personnel and people, they would enter, supervise, they would provide health care for all those who needed it, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reports that you would receive them, either informally or formally, however the information that was communicated to you by these individuals, you then reported to the Minister of Defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, you asked me whom I was under in the ministry, whom -- who was under me in the ministry. You didn't even ask me who was under me in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I will first of all have to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you didn't answer me but if you'd like to tell me now, I would welcome the information.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what I should answer. I've already told you. You didn't even ask me who my subordinates were in the field so how are you going to know what you're asking me? And how should I know how to answer that question, unless I don't tell you who was responsibility to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise but I think it is time for me to intervene. It is obvious that the Prosecution is expressing his antagonism towards this witness and the witness can feel that. I don't think it is necessary, the responsibility for the witness's questions, well the Prosecutor is responsible for this, if he asks such questions, he can expect such answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't sense any antagonism at this moment. Mr. Scott, you may ask that question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not going to take you back in the transcript to where I asked you this before so I'll ask you again. Who was your direct subordinates in the HVO Ministry of Defence, whether they were in Mostar, whether they were in the field, who were those people who directly reported to you as their superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said who they were with in the HVO structure in the ministry. In the field, these people were the heads of war hospitals and they were also the commanders of certain regions, military districts. But they provided me with medical reports, reports which had to do with health care. And these reports and all other reports, if they were necessary, well, they were responsible to their commanders, the commanders of units in the field, and in professional terms, for the implementation of health care, they were responsible to the health administration, to the chief, to the head, to the chief medical headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And with that information that came to you, you reported that information on to the Minister for Defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing again. Yes and no. When it had to do with something which was part of my responsibility, I was responsible to deal with it, then it wasn't necessary for me to contact the minister to report to the Minister. I would deal with it. That's why I was his assistant but for sort of overall acts, overall requests, general requests, I didn't come to decisions on my own. I had to inform the Minister of this. And ask for his agreement. Among other things, when -- if we are talking about that hospital or certain activities such as the delivery of humanitarian aid through convoys, with which doctors were sent, or doctors sent negotiation teams, et cetera, et cetera. Well obviously the Minister had to be informed of this and there had to be an agreement, he had to it agree to such matters. So that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like if the usher could show you please Exhibit P578.11. P578.11 and the same time you can please show him 578.12.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are very, very short documents that are only in B/C/S but there is only one sentence that need be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that as shown on both of these documents, one is indicating it was signed by Valentin Coric, the head of the military police of the HVO and the other one, 578.12 being signed by a man named Ivan Anjic [phoen]. You were one of nine people in the entire HVO military structure, you were one of only nine people who could give freedom of movement throughout Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout Herceg-Bosna? Anyone who was in Herceg-Bosna had the right to move freely throughout Herceg-Bosna. I would first of all have to read through these documents. And comment on them. But as I said, anyone could move freely through Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention and I'll ask the interpreters to help us, please. I'm look at 578.11, after the preparatory lines and then there is a title in the middle of the page starting with the letter Z, the paragraph then that follows, and before the list of nine names, sir, can you read that to us, please, very slowly and clearly so that we can get the English interpretation? Would you please read that? Can you read it out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but I would like to ask you why do I have to read this out loud? Can I read it for myself, first of all?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask the interpreters, Your Honour, if it will assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we don't have the English translations, so if you would be kind enough to read it out loud so that we could understand what it's about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Very well. I understand you. Thank you very much. Well, "At all border crossings and throughout the territory which is under the control of the HVO military police, ensure freedom of movement without hindrance for transports, foreign journalists, employees of humanitarian organisations, and all other citizens on whose permits for movement, for free movement, you can find the following names." Shall I read through the names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary, sir, the Judges can read the names, including Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petskovic and others. And you, sir, being one of the nine, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document and I wouldn't like to comment on it, I wouldn't like to say anything about it. I never received this document, but I would like to say the following: Probably given my constant requests to make this possible, this thing possible, that thing possible, to implement this thing and to do that thing, et cetera, et cetera, well, if this document is correct, it's probably for this reason that people said, okay whatever Ivan Bagaric says should be done, should be implemented and whatever he signs we should try to make it possible for this to be implemented. And therefore -- well at the time I was the assistant of the head of the Defence department or later the Minister of Defence so that's how I understand this, although I've never seen this and I wasn't aware that such a document had been written. I wasn't aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think you've told us yet either in direct examination unless I missed it which is always possible, or in cross-examination, who put you in this position or named you or appointed you? Who put you in the position of assistant Minister of Defence for medical services?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just in order to clarify something, the Prosecutor said Minister of Defence but what we heard was the head of the Defence department. That's what entered the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript says exactly the -- put the position of assistant Minister of Defence for medical services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is the interpretation we got through the earphones. I don't want the witness to be confused. The head of the Defence department. That's what the interpretation said. That's what we heard. Well that is the Defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Honours it's very important because in the HZ HB, and the Prosecutor knows this as well as you do, there were departments and in the HZ HB, there were ministries. I don't think there is anything in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who named you, sir to the position you held from approximately, as you've told us, September of 1992, through at least the year 1993? Who put you in that position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was appointed by what was the name of it? By the executive branch of the government under the HVO control, so the highest person in the executive branch, whether it was the Minister or somebody else, I don't know, but that arose from my position in the parliament and then the doctor so I could not be appointed as the head of the army or -- I really do not know who appointed me, but I was appointed. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to press you on this. This is an extremely senior position. The most senior medical officer in the entire HVO military. I'm going to suggest to you, sir, you surely must know who put you in that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. position.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not one of the highest. It was the highest position in the military structure of the health care of the HVO. So that was the leading position. And also a position of an assistant minister. Whether I was appointed by the Defence Minister or the body that was not the government at the time but representatives of the executive branch of the government in the area that was still under the control of the HVO, I don't know. And I don't know how else to answer your question. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many times did you meet with anyone on behalf of Mr. Naletilic prior to giving your testimony in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I was not concentrating. Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely. How many times, sir, before beginning your testimony on Tuesday did you meet with anyone on behalf of Mr. Naletilic in connection with your giving testimony here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, let us hear the answer from the witness first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met with representatives of Mr. Krsnik's office just one time. I met with them last summer, from somebody with Mr. Krsnik's office. And they inquired about some general circumstances surrounding my future testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you describe to them what you knew and what it was that you could possibly testify about? Did you talk about a statement that you might make or the information that you could provide to them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was asked whether I would be willing, if the -- either the Tribunal, the Chamber, or somebody else decided that it was necessary for me to come and give my testimony about what I know and what I did during the war, as the head of the medical services, and I said I did, and I am here and I offer my cooperation to this Tribunal at any time whenever my cooperation is needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your position, then, sir, that prior to taking the witness stand on Tuesday, you had never provided any information to anyone on behalf of Mr. Naletilic about what your testimony would be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for that one time when I mentioned, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well did anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise if I am wrong but I believe that once somebody says on behalf of Mr. Naletilic, my learned friend should be correct and say with the Defence for Mr. Naletilic, because I don't know what it means, on behalf of Mr. Naletilic. It could have been his sister. So why didn't he say exactly who he meant whether he said on behalf of Mr. Naletilic. This serves just to confuse the witness. He could have said the Defence. And another thing, Your Honours, something that -- but I didn't want to intervene. When somebody says, "I have four documents," and the following day you turn up with 20 documents so that maybe the Defence would not do something overnight like the case was with another witness whose name I cannot mention because he was protected, so one day, somebody says four documents, the following day they turn up with 20 documents, and that -- so much about the correct behaviour of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, are you going to tell us something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. I believe I understand Mr. Prosecutor now. I understand the question. As God is my witness, I -- nobody on behalf of Mr. Naletilic or anybody else, that is relatives, friends, have ever spoken to me about this, nor have I provided anybody with any information, except for that one time when people from Mr. Krsnik's office asked me and when I said that I am at their disposal and the disposal of this Trial Chamber if they may decide that I can explain some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I thought that, not as long as you understand the question, but now I realise that you did not understand the question. Yes, Mr. Scott, I believe that we finished this part of the question. Would you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court would allow me one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did meet on this one instance, you've now told us sir a couple of times that this was only the one time, how long did this conversation or meeting last? Was it five minutes or several hours or how long?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you sincerely if that is your last question, because this gives me hope that I will be home for the weekend. I sincerely thank you, and I invite you to come to Bosnia. I would like to show Bosnia to you. And then maybe a lot more things would be clear to you, and I understand why some things are not clear because you are not from Bosnia. So that one time, I think it was ten minutes, ten minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to disappoint you, sir, but I didn't suggest that that was going to be my last question except in response to the President that I would move off that topic with that question. I would like the usher, please, to show you Exhibit P239.11. I have a feeling it's -- I'm sorry, that's right. P239.11. Sir, I'd like you to look at that for a moment, please, and perhaps the English version could be placed on the ELMO. This appears to be an order issued by Bruno Stojic, the Minister of Defence or to use the exact words interpreted here head of the HZ HB Defence department, about the reporting of casualty information. And you were listed or indicated at least in the English translation, on the top part of the second page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that and I'm -- I am aware of this document. I'm not aware of this specific document but I know its source and origin and I know why it was issued, and I can explain that to you, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is in fact my next question, sir. Can you tell the Judges, please, what the circumstances were leading Minister Stojic to issue this order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the so-called chief medical headquarters, later on health administration, we had a department that monitored the sufferings of both civilians and soldiers so we had a data base containing the names of the dead, of the wounded, so we could monitor their treatment, their medical care provided to them, their whereabouts, whether they were discharged, then the head of that department was Dr. Marija Brajko and at one instance, she prepared various documents that we sent to the ground from this area, and on one occasion, she asked to have an insight into the matter because this was requested of her from the human rights centre. So she wanted to be provided with the information on all those who perished in that particular way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, on a few minutes that we have left this evening, let me just ask you a couple of questions. At the beginning of the document, it says this: "If there is a suspicion that a war crime has been committed, or that someone was killed with cold steel, tortured or mutilated, whether the victims are children, civilians or soldiers, a post-mortem must be performed." Can you tell the Judges was that the procedure to your knowledge that was widely followed or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, at this moment, I don't know to what extent was this procedure followed, but I know that the objective was to collect information on the victims, on the sufferings, and that the doctor that I mentioned was in charge of that, she was affiliated with that particular department for a while, and her goal was to write a book. I don't know what the topic of the book would have been because she never published the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were the superior of this woman, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At her request, I could not issue an order to military units, because I was not their commander. So I suggested that Mr. Stojic should do that, and I don't see anything strange about this document. Yes, I was her superior, the superior of Dr. Brncic as well as all the of those who were affiliated with the health care system at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir at the bottom of this document, I'm sorry, at least on the bottom of the first page of the English version, the English translation, it says this: "All such cases must be reported to the information and investigation unit of the health care sector of the Defence department." So since you were, as you told us a number of times now, the most senior officer in the entire HVO medical department, and since this woman who was give then responsibility was your immediate, direct subordinate, tell the Chamber, please, was this procedure followed or not? Was it information about victims of war crimes kept and maintained or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, all such cases must be reported to the information and investigation unit of the health care sector of the Defence department. So this was the unit which, at the very beginning, was set up as a firm structure in charge of collecting information, compiling a database, providing information. Whether this was followed through or not, I don't know. It would be good if it had been but I believe it wasn't because Dr. Brncic never wrote a book that she promised she would do, based on all the information that she was collecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very simple. Are these all the documents that my learned friend is going to use or are we to expect a new pile of documents to arrive at our desk on Monday? Because it was your order that after the solemn oath is taken that the documents should be given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sure it is the substantial majority of the documents. Now, the Rule as I understand the Chamber has put into practice is to facilitate and as an aid if in the course of the cross-examination, an additional document comes to my attention yes, we may have an additional document or two on Monday morning and I don't understand any of the Chamber's Rulings to prohibit that. We are provide the documents as an aid when the cross-examination starts. Not that those will be the only documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I'm sorry, we have to keep you here in The Hague over the weekend. I have to remind you that during the period you are in The Hague, you are still under the solemn declaration. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. I am really sorry that we did not find just a little bit more time and bring my testimony to the end, because if the Mr. Prosecutor is going to be honest, then he will admit that there are not so many questions that he can put to me from which he can derive at this or that conclusion. And if you can order him to continue his cross-examination, now, please do so. I would kindly ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think it's proper for you to judge the results of the questions asked by the Prosecution. But any way, we will resume Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
